blocks.text: Ashgabat, *Aşgabat* in Turkmen, is the capital of Turkmenistan and by far its largest city. It lies in an oasis at the northern foot of the Kopetdag mountains, on the edge of the Karakum desert, about 30 km from the border with Iran.

People lived at the foot of these mountains long before the city existed. About 18 km to the west are the ruins of Nisa, which UNESCO describes as one of the earliest and most important cities of the Parthian Empire, a great power from the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE. Its fortresses have been a World Heritage Site since 2007.

The modern city began in 1881 as a Russian military fort, named after the nearby Turkmen settlement of Askhabad. After the Russian Revolution it was called Poltoratsk for a few years and became Ashkhabad again in 1927; from 1924 it was the capital of the Turkmen Soviet republic. Turkmenistan adopted the Turkmen spelling, Ashgabat, in 1992.

In the early hours of 6 October 1948, an earthquake of magnitude 7.3 struck about 25 km from the city. Built mostly of mud brick or fired brick, nearly every building collapsed or was damaged beyond repair. Soviet censorship kept the news quiet, and the number of dead is still uncertain: estimates range from about 10,000 to 110,000, the figure the United States Geological Survey gives. The city was rebuilt on its old street plan. For a long time water was scarce, until the Karakum Canal reached Ashgabat in 1962.

Today Ashgabat is the country's centre of government, industry and culture. Britannica lists carpet-weaving and cotton mills among its industries, and an opera house, theatres and several museums among its institutions. The Academy of Sciences, founded in 1951, includes an Institute of Deserts: a fitting neighbour for the Karakum.

Since the 1990s, much of the centre has been rebuilt again, with wide avenues and white stone. In 2013 Guinness World Records listed Ashgabat as the city with the highest density of buildings clad in white marble: 543 buildings in an area of 22 square kilometres.

blocks.title: In Ashgabat
blocks.text: Turkmen writes no apostrophe before an ending, so the name of the city simply grows: *Aşgabat*, *Aşgabatda* (in Ashgabat), *Aşgabatly* (from Ashgabat).
With the words of this unit, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Aşgabat Türkmenistanda. Aşgabat uly we owadan şäher. Bu şäherde ak jaý köp. Muzeý hem, seýilgäh hem bar.
blocks.en: Ashgabat is in Turkmenistan. Ashgabat is a big and beautiful city. There are many white buildings in this city. There are museums and parks too.

questions.q: What happened to Ashgabat in October 1948?
options: An earthquake destroyed most of the city
The ruins of Parthian fortresses near Ashgabat
A new district of marble buildings

questions.explain: The back vowel *a* gives *-da*, written straight onto the name with no apostrophe.

sources.title: Ashgabat
sources.note: Oasis at the northern foot of the Kopet-Dag, about 30 km from Iran; founded in 1881 as a Russian military fort named after the settlement of Askhabad; Poltoratsk, Ashkhabad again in 1927; capital from 1924; Ashgabat spelling in 1992; the October 1948 earthquake and rebuilding on the same plan; the Karakum Canal in 1962; industries, opera house, theatres, museums; the Academy of Sciences (1951) and its Institute of Deserts

sources.title: Parthian Fortresses of Nisa
sources.note: One of the earliest and most important cities of the Parthian Empire, a major power from the mid 3rd century BC to the 3rd century AD; inscribed in 2007

sources.title: 1948 Ashgabat earthquake
sources.note: Magnitude 7.3 on 6 October, epicentre about 25 km south-west of the city; adobe and fired-brick buildings nearly all collapsed or were damaged beyond repair; Soviet censorship; death toll estimates from 10,000 to 110,000 (USGS PAGER-CAT)

sources.title: Highest density of white marble-clad buildings
sources.note: Ashgabat, 25 March 2013: 543 buildings in 22 km², 4,513,584 m² of white marble
